overview.title: Loading and splitting the English-Spanish dataset
overview.main_topic: Downloading spa-eng.zip, parsing tab-separated English/Spanish sentence pairs, wrapping each Spanish target in [start] ... [end] tokens, and making a shuffled 70/15/15 train/validation/test split
overview.central_idea: A translation dataset is a list of (source, target) sentence pairs. The target is wrapped in explicit start and end markers so a decoder can later be seeded with [start] and know to stop at [end]; the pairs are shuffled and split before any tokenizer is fitted.
overview.importance: This data is used for every translation model in the chapter: the RNN seq2seq model (15.2.2) and the Transformer (15.3.4). The [start]/[end] convention directly implements the inference procedure of Figure 15.1.
learning_objectives: Download and locate a dataset with keras.utils.get_file
Parse a tab-separated parallel corpus into (english, spanish) pairs
Explain why the Spanish target gets [start] and [end] but the English source does not
Compute the split sizes: 15% validation, 15% test, 70% training
Explain why the shuffle happens before the split
prerequisites: Basic Python string and list operations

summary:
Section 15.2.1 starts the translation example with an **English-to-Spanish** dataset.

1. **Download**: `keras.utils.get_file` fetches `spa-eng.zip` from `storage.googleapis.com`, extracts it (`extract=True`), and `text_path` points to `spa-eng/spa.txt` inside the extracted folder.
2. **Parse**: the file holds one example per line: *English sentence, a tab, the Spanish sentence*. The code reads the file, splits on `"\n"` and drops the last (empty) element with `[:-1]`. Each line is split on `"\t"`; the Spanish side is rewritten as `"[start] " + spanish + " [end]"` and the pair is appended to `text_pairs`.
3. **Inspect**: a random pair looks like `("Who is in this room?", "[start] ¿Quién está en esta habitación? [end]")`.
4. **Split**: after `random.shuffle(text_pairs)`, `val_samples = int(0.15 * len(text_pairs))`, `train_samples = len(text_pairs) - 2 * val_samples`; the list is sliced into `train_pairs` (~70%), `val_pairs` (15%) and `test_pairs` (the remaining ~15%).

The page ends by announcing **two separate `TextVectorization` layers**, one per language, with customized string preprocessing (detailed on p.455).

Why the markers? Following Figure 15.1 (p.453), the decoder is seeded with `"[start]"` at inference time and generation stops when it emits `"[end]"`. Only the target (Spanish) needs them, because only the target is generated; the English source is simply encoded.

paragraphs.excerpt: We’ll be working with an English-to-Spanish translation dataset. Let’s download it:
paragraphs.what_it_says: The example uses an English-to-Spanish translation dataset, downloaded with the code below.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `get_file` downloads once and caches the file (by default under `~/.keras/datasets`), and `extract=True` unzips it. `pathlib.Path(zip_path) / "spa-eng" / "spa.txt"` builds the path to the text file inside the extracted directory.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A parallel corpus (aligned sentence pairs) is the supervised data a translation model needs.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the exact directory layout returned by get_file with extract=True has changed across Keras versions; if `spa.txt` is not found, print `zip_path` and inspect the folder.

terminology.meaning: A dataset of sentences paired with their translations.

paragraphs.excerpt: The text file contains one example per line: an English sentence, followed by
paragraphs.what_it_says: Each line is an English sentence, a tab, and the Spanish translation; the code parses the file into pairs and wraps the Spanish side in [start] and [end].
paragraphs.what_it_means: `f.read().split("\n")[:-1]` produces one string per line and discards the empty string after the final newline. `line.split("\t")` separates the two languages. Adding `"[start] "` and `" [end]"` (note the spaces) makes them separate whitespace tokens after tokenization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These markers are what the decoder will learn to produce and condition on. At training time the decoder input begins with [start]; the target sequence (shifted by one) ends with [end] (p.455-456).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): `english, spanish = line.split("\t")` assumes exactly two fields per line; if a version of the file had extra columns (such as attribution), the unpacking would fail and you'd use `line.split("\t")[:2]`.

terminology.meaning: Special tokens marking the beginning and end of a target sequence for the decoder.

connections: p.453: Figure 15.1, seed token [start] and stop token [end]

paragraphs.what_it_says: A random example: ("Who is in this room?", "[start] ¿Quién está en esta habitación? [end]").
paragraphs.what_it_means: The source keeps its original case and punctuation; the target has the markers and Spanish punctuation such as ¿. Both will be standardized by the tokenizers on p.455.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Looking at raw samples reveals preprocessing needs, e.g. the inverted question mark that string.punctuation does not cover.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s shuffle them and split them into the usual training, validation, and test sets:
paragraphs.what_it_says: The pairs are shuffled and split into training, validation and test sets.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Validation and test each get `int(0.15 * N)` pairs; training gets the rest, about 70%. Slicing is contiguous, so shuffling first is what makes each split a random sample.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The file is likely ordered (e.g. by sentence length); without shuffling, the test set would contain only the longest sentences. The tokenizers are later fitted on train_pairs only, avoiding information leakage.
paragraphs.technical_idea: random.shuffle is unseeded here, so the split differs between runs; call random.seed(...) first for reproducibility (not in the book).

terminology.meaning: Partitioning data into disjoint training, validation and test subsets.

connections: p.455: tokenizers adapted on train_pairs only

paragraphs.excerpt: Next, let’s prepare two separate `TextVectorization` layers: one for English and one for
paragraphs.what_it_says: Two separate TextVectorization layers will be prepared, one per language, with customized string preprocessing.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each language gets its own vocabulary, since the encoder reads English IDs and the decoder reads and predicts Spanish IDs. The customization (continued on p.455) keeps [ and ] and strips ¿ for Spanish.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Separate vocabularies keep each embedding table and the decoder's output softmax limited to the relevant language.

terminology.meaning: Keras layer that standardizes, splits and indexes text (chapter 14).

concepts.name: Sequence-to-sequence data
concepts.definition: Training data consisting of (source sequence, target sequence) pairs.
concepts.intuition: Question and answer, sentence and translation.
concepts.technical: Here a list of (English string, '[start] Spanish [end]') tuples.
concepts.significance: Defines what the encoder reads and what the decoder must generate.
concepts.example: ("Who is in this room?", "[start] ¿Quién está en esta habitación? [end]").
concepts.misconception: Source and target need not have the same length.

concepts.name: Start and end tokens
concepts.definition: Marker tokens that signal the start and end of a generated sequence.
concepts.technical: Inserted as text, preserved through standardization (p.455), and assigned their own vocabulary IDs.
concepts.significance: Enable seeding generation and deciding when to stop.
concepts.example: The decoder is fed [start] first and loops until it outputs [end] (p.453).
concepts.misconception: They are not added to the source sentence; only the target is generated.

concepts.name: Train/validation/test split
concepts.definition: Disjoint subsets for fitting, model selection and final evaluation.
concepts.intuition: Practice questions, mock exam, real exam.
concepts.significance: Gives an unbiased estimate of translation quality.
concepts.misconception: Shuffling after slicing would not randomize which examples go to test.

math.source_text: val_samples = int(0.15 * len(text_pairs)); train_samples = len(text_pairs) - 2 * val_samples

code.title: Downloading the English-Spanish dataset
code.original_code:
import pathlib
zip_path = keras.utils.get_file(
    origin=(
        "http://storage.googleapis.com/download.tensorflow.org/data/spa-eng.zip"
    ),
    fname="spa-eng",
    extract=True,
)
text_path = pathlib.Path(zip_path) / "spa-eng" / "spa.txt"
code.what_it_does: Downloads and extracts spa-eng.zip and builds the path to spa.txt.

line_explanations.explanation: get_file downloads (and caches) the archive under the name spa-eng and extracts it.
Path to the tab-separated text file.

pitfalls: Directory layout of the extracted archive can differ between Keras versions.

code.title: Parsing sentence pairs and adding start/end tokens
code.original_code:
with open(text_path) as f:
    lines = f.read().split("\n")[:-1]
text_pairs = []
for line in lines:
    english, spanish = line.split("\t")
    spanish = "[start] " + spanish + " [end]"
    text_pairs.append((english, spanish))
code.what_it_does: Reads spa.txt into a list of (english, '[start] spanish [end]') tuples.

line_explanations.explanation: Read the whole file and split into lines, dropping the trailing empty string.
Split each line at the tab into source and target.
Wrap the target in start/end markers, separated by spaces so they become separate tokens.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: text file. Output: text_pairs list.
code.theory_link: Implements the seed/stop convention of Figure 15.1.
pitfalls: open() without encoding='utf-8' relies on the platform default; on some systems accented characters may be decoded incorrectly (not discussed in the book).
A line with more than one tab would break the two-way unpacking.

code.title: Inspecting a random pair
code.original_code:
>>> import random
>>> random.choice(text_pairs)
("Who is in this room?", "[start] ¿Quién está en esta habitación? [end]")

line_explanations.explanation: random.choice picks one tuple; the output shows the markers around the Spanish sentence.

code.title: Shuffling and splitting the pairs
code.original_code:
import random
random.shuffle(text_pairs)
val_samples = int(0.15 * len(text_pairs))
train_samples = len(text_pairs) - 2 * val_samples
train_pairs = text_pairs[:train_samples]
val_pairs = text_pairs[train_samples : train_samples + val_samples]
test_pairs = text_pairs[train_samples + val_samples :]
code.what_it_does: Shuffles in place and slices into train (~70%), validation (15%) and test (15%).

line_explanations.explanation: Contiguous slices of the shuffled list.

parameters.role: Fraction for validation and for test.

pitfalls: Unseeded shuffle: different split each run.
Exact-duplicate sentence pairs may land in both train and test.

deeper.title: How the markers will be used
deeper.body: On p.455-456 the Spanish string is tokenized to `sequence_length + 1 = 21` IDs. The decoder **input** is the first 20 (starting with [start]); the **target** is the last 20 (ending with [end], then padding). At inference the decoder receives only [start], predicts a word, appends it, and repeats until it predicts [end] (Figure 15.1, p.453).

deeper.title: Why separate source and target treatment
deeper.body: The English sentence is only *read* (encoded), so it needs no markers. The Spanish sentence is both *read* (teacher forcing: the decoder sees previous target tokens) and *predicted*, so it needs a defined starting input and a defined end.

deeper.title: Analogy: a relay baton
deeper.body: [start] is the starter's pistol that tells the decoder to run its first leg; [end] is the finish line. Without a finish line, generation would run until an arbitrary length cap.

misconceptions.claim: Both source and target need [start] and [end].
misconceptions.correction: Only the target, which the decoder generates, is wrapped.

misconceptions.claim: The test set is defined by its own 0.15 calculation.
misconceptions.correction: It is the remainder after train and validation, which equals int(0.15 N) by construction.

misconceptions.claim: It doesn't matter whether you shuffle before slicing.
misconceptions.correction: Slicing an ordered file would give non-representative splits.

takeaways: The dataset is a tab-separated file of English/Spanish sentence pairs.
Each Spanish target is wrapped as '[start] ... [end]' for the decoder.
Pairs are shuffled, then split 15% validation, 15% test, ~70% training.
Two separate TextVectorization layers will tokenize English and Spanish.

questions.question: Why are [start] and [end] added only to the Spanish sentences?
options: Spanish is the target sequence the decoder generates
The English tokenizer cannot handle brackets
To make the sentences equal in length
questions.answer: Spanish is the target sequence the decoder generates
questions.explanation: The decoder needs a seed token and a stop token (Figure 15.1). Punctuation, bracket handling and length equalization are not the reason.

questions.question: With 20,000 pairs, how many go to training, validation and test?
What does [:-1] do in `f.read().split("\n")[:-1]`?
questions.answer: Drops the empty string that follows the file's final newline.

questions.question: Why must the shuffle precede the slicing?
questions.answer: Slices are contiguous; without shuffling, each split would inherit the file's ordering and not be a random sample.

questions.question: Why are spaces included in "[start] " and " [end]"?
questions.answer: So that the markers become separate tokens when the text is split on whitespace.

questions.question: Could you explain how the [start] token will be used at inference time?
questions.answer: The decoder receives [start] plus the encoded source, predicts the first word, feeds it back, and loops until [end].
